t: Introduction: why histopathological features are needed
n: In this lecture we will consider the forensic medical significance of histopathological features. A change found under the microscope may be the cause of death, or it may be an incidental finding unrelated to death. Inflammation of the heart, that is myocarditis, is often found at autopsy, but its histological diagnosis is difficult. Diffuse alveolar damage, DAD, is a multifactorial change, and determining the cause of death from it alone is not to be expected. Histology alone is not sufficient. Pre-mortem medical and forensic medical data, toxicology and analysis of the circumstances are also needed.

t: Lecture plan and two main sources
n: The lecture consists of two parts. The first part is devoted to the lung: diffuse alveolar damage, its stages and causes of death; the source is Urer and colleagues, 2012. The second part is devoted to the heart: myocardial inflammation and its significance in death; the source is du Long and colleagues, 2022. The du Long study examined forensic and clinical autopsies together, 79 cases in all.

t: Diffuse alveolar damage (DAD): definition
n: Diffuse alveolar damage, DAD, is the morphological prototype of acute interstitial pneumonia. Its course is rapid and may lead to death. Clinically, DAD presents as acute respiratory distress syndrome, that is ARDS. It occurs in sepsis, shock, trauma and in acute exacerbation of chronic interstitial lung diseases. On X-ray, bilateral diffuse opacification is seen, and profound hypoxaemia requires artificial ventilation. Mortality is 43–50%.

t: In which conditions DAD occurs
n: In which conditions DAD occurs. DAD is the morphological prototype of acute interstitial pneumonia, the course of which is rapid and catastrophic. It occurs in systemic conditions, that is sepsis and shock, in injury, that is trauma, and in acute respiratory distress syndrome. It is also seen when the cause is unclear, in idiopathic cases. In addition, it occurs in acute exacerbation of chronic interstitial lung diseases.

t: The role of forensic autopsy in studying DAD
n: The role of forensic autopsy in studying DAD. In patients with severe respiratory failure, open lung biopsy is limited, so such data are scarce. In the acute stage the risk of death is high, so biopsy more often finds the late or organising stage. Open biopsy in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis may trigger an acute exacerbation. Therefore forensic autopsy and the study of the distribution of DAD may be an alternative direction of research.

t: Quick question 1: basics of DAD
n: The first quick question. Question: of which disease is DAD the morphological prototype? Answer: acute interstitial pneumonia. Question: with which syndrome does DAD present clinically? Answer: acute respiratory distress syndrome, ARDS. Attention: risk of error — DAD and ARDS are not the same thing. DAD is a morphological picture, whereas ARDS is a clinical syndrome. In radiology, bilateral diffuse opacification and profound hypoxaemia, in most cases requiring mechanical ventilation, are seen.

t: Material and method of the study (Urer et al.)
n: Material and method of the study, after Urer and colleagues. In 2006–2008, 12,504 autopsies were performed; 6813 had a histological specimen. Sixty-six persons over 18 with a diagnosis of diffuse alveolar damage were selected. Lung preparations stained with haematoxylin and eosin, H&E, were re-assessed by a pathologist under a light microscope. The Fisher test and regression were used in the analysis. The sequence of stages is as follows: autopsies, histological reports, cases with DAD, review of the preparations, statistical analysis.

t: ATS/ERS criteria and grades of assessment
n: The assessment is based on the 2002 ATS/ERS consensus criteria, that is of the American Thoracic Society and the European Respiratory Society. Features were assessed on a scale of 0 absent, 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3 severe. By intensity, chronic inflammation and eosinophilia are assessed, and by extent, hyaline membrane, both on a scale of 0–3. The main criterion is alveolar organising fibrosis. Its presence or absence separates the exudative from the proliferative phase.

t: Phases of DAD: exudative, proliferative, fibrotic
n: DAD passes through three stages: early exudative, subacute proliferative and late fibrotic. The exudative phase is the acute phase; in the study 50 cases, that is 75.7%, were in this phase. The proliferative phase is subacute: hyaline membrane forms 4–5 days after injury and was more frequent in proliferative cases. In this phase there were 16 cases, that is 24.2%. The fibrotic phase is the late, chronic phase.

t: Appearance and frequency of hyaline membrane (HM)
n: Hyaline membrane, HM, begins to be seen 4–5 days after injury. According to Ferrer, HM was found in 12% of cases in the exudative phase and in 62% of those in the proliferative phase. In this study too, HM was more frequent in the proliferative phase than in the exudative phase. That is, the frequency of hyaline membrane rises as the phases progress.

t: Results: phases and demographic indicators
n: Results. Of the 66 cases with a diagnosis of diffuse alveolar damage, 50, that is 75.7%, were in the exudative phase and 16, that is 24.2%, in the proliferative phase. Of the cases, 55, that is 83.3%, were men and 11, that is 16.6%, were women. The mean age was 53, the median 54 years; the age range was 19 to 92.

t: Histological features distinguishing the phases
n: Histological features distinguishing the phases. Only alveolar exudate or oedema was significantly higher in the exudative phase, P value 0.003. In the proliferative phase there was more histiocytic desquamation, fibrosis, chronic inflammation and fibrin; their P values were 0.037, 0.017, 0.02 and 0.001. In regression, only alveolar fibrin independently predicted the proliferative phase, P = 0.016.

t: Quick question 2: phases and features
n: The second quick question. Question: which feature became an independent variable in favour of the proliferative phase in logistic regression? Answer: alveolar fibrin, P = 0.016. In the exudative phase only the proportion of alveolar exudate or oedema was significantly higher, P = 0.003. In proliferative cases, the following were more frequent: alveolar histiocytic desquamation, alveolar fibrosis, chronic inflammation and fibrin. Attention: fibrosis and chronic inflammation were frequent in the proliferative phase, but mild in degree. The independent feature is only fibrin.

t: Causes of DAD: trauma and fire predominate
n: Causes of DAD. Twenty-eight cases, that is 41%, were associated with physical trauma. Seven of them were road traffic and industrial accidents. The most frequent types of incident were physical trauma and fire. No difference by phase was found between the trauma, burn and other groups. Fat embolism developed after trauma was identified in one case of DAD in the proliferative phase. Of DAD deaths at forensic autopsy, 92% are unnatural, with trauma the commonest cause. In hospital series, by contrast, infection predominates.

t: Case analysis: DAD and the cause of death
n: Case analysis on DAD and the cause of death. Situation: DAD is found under the microscope in the lungs of a person who died after trauma or fire. The situation is based on the types of case in the study. Question: does DAD alone determine the cause of death? No. DAD is a general change caused by many factors, so it alone cannot be the cause. Pre-mortem medical and forensic medical data should be assessed together. In a fire, hypoxia and combustion gases play an important role. Attention: the absence of DAD at autopsy does not exclude ARDS, since DAD is found in only half of those with ARDS clinically.

t: Pulmonary and extrapulmonary DAD
n: Pulmonary and extrapulmonary DAD. Pulmonary DAD arises from a pathological insult within the alveolus, for example pneumonia. Extrapulmonary DAD arises from systemic inflammation, for example sepsis, and from injury caused by circulating cytokines. No difference in the distribution of hyaline membrane between the two groups was reported: although the development differs, the pathological changes are similar. The forensic series includes cases of both kinds; DAD after fire may be associated with pulmonary or extrapulmonary risk.

t: Differential diagnosis: DAD ≠ similar conditions
n: Differential diagnosis. Making a microscopic differential diagnosis is more important than relating the mechanism to the histology. Hyaline membrane was present in all cases, so the variant of acute fibrinous pneumonia did not fit; in fibrinous pneumonia there is no HM and fibrin accumulates widely. In bacterial pneumonia there are many neutrophils, whereas in DAD there are few. In an exacerbation of UIP there is patchy fibrosis and a honeycomb pattern. If septal fibrosis and alveolar organising fibrosis are combined, this is a sign of the proliferative phase.

t: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia and UIP exacerbation
n: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia and UIP exacerbation. In an exacerbation of UIP there is a histological reaction resembling DAD, but patchy interstitial fibrosis and a honeycomb pattern are found in the background. In the study, chronic inflammatory cells and fibrosis of the alveolar septa were mild; no case met the criteria for UIP exacerbation. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia, AEP, causes: toxic inhalation, drug reactions, infection, parasites, mycoses, smoking. In one case of death from burns there was moderate eosinophilic infiltration; the absence of microabscesses, diffuse HM and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia excluded AEP.

t: Mechanisms of lung injury
n: Mechanisms of lung injury. In trauma, head injury, respiratory muscles and pulmonary artery pressure are also important; hypoxia from bleeding, cytokines and oedema play a role. In fire, hypoxia and gases released in combustion act. Abdominal and chest surgery is particularly dangerous: anaesthesia and disturbance of chest movement have an effect. Chemotherapy agents, some antibiotics and paraquat can give a complication of alveolar damage; here there is a toxic effect on the alveoli, acidosis and cytokines.

t: Attention: limitations of DAD and diagnostic value
n: Attention: limitations of DAD and diagnostic value. DAD is a general change arising from different factors, so by itself it does not determine the cause of death. Pre-mortem medical and forensic medical data are assessed together. DAD is found at autopsy in only half of people with ARDS clinically. The absence of DAD does not exclude ARDS. Limitations of the study: alveolar haemorrhage was not assessed, the data were taken from reports, intervals before death and intervention are unknown, and there is inter-observer variation. The mechanism of development of DAD is not fully understood, so the pathologist and forensic specialist must also know the clinical parameters.

t: Quick question 3: end of the DAD section
n: The third quick question, the end of the DAD section. Question: if diffuse alveolar damage is found in the lungs, is the cause of death determined by that? Why are ante-mortem and forensic medical data assessed together? Answer: DAD is not characteristic of a single disease. It is a general pathological change that may arise from different factors. Therefore determining the cause of death from DAD alone is not to be expected. Attention: DAD is found in about half of those with ARDS clinically. The absence of DAD does not exclude ARDS.

t: Myocardial inflammation: statement of the problem
n: Now the second part: myocardial inflammation. Myocarditis is frequently found at forensic and clinical autopsies. In studies of sudden cardiac death the frequency of occurrence is from 0.3% to 14.8%. The histopathological diagnosis of myocarditis is difficult. Clinically it varies from mild "flu-like" signs to sudden death. When other findings are also present, it is hard to assess whether the inflammation is the cause of death, a contributing factor or an insignificant finding. For example, myocarditis may coincide with findings consistent with asphyxia from strangulation or restraint, or with borderline lethal toxicology.

t: Study design and selection (du Long et al.)
n: Study design and selection, du Long and colleagues. This is a retrospective, two-centre study: forensic and clinical autopsy cases, 2014–2019. Excluded were: those under 18, those with systemic or ischaemic heart disease, and an incomplete report or block. In the end 79 cases remained: 41 forensic, 38 clinical; 56 men, 23 women.

t: Structure of the three groups
n: Structure of the three groups. A total of 79 adult autopsies were studied: 41 forensic and 38 clinical cases. Group 1 had 27 cases with clearly unnatural death; myocarditis was assessed as an incidental finding, and the patients lived less than 1 hour. Group 2 had 29 cases: myocarditis was one of the possible causes. Group 3 had 23 cases: myocarditis was the only significant finding. No one in groups 2 and 3 had undergone successful resuscitation.

t: Focus of inflammation and histological features
n: Focus of inflammation and histological features. A focus is a collection of at least 10 inflammatory cells. On H&E-stained sections the number and location of foci were counted. If there were no clear foci but inflammatory cells were scattered, the case was recorded as "diffuse". Myocyte damage is vacuolation, fragmentation or disintegration of the cardiomyocyte next to inflammatory cells. Fibrosis, oedema and haemorrhage were recorded as present or absent. Attention: only diffuse inflammation reliably distinguished the groups. Myocyte damage, oedema, fibrosis and haemorrhage turned out almost equal in the groups.

t: Inflammation index (Kitulwatte)
n: Inflammation index, after Kitulwatte. The index equals the total number of foci divided by the total number of sections. The values are as follows: 0 no inflammation, and 0 also in diffuse; 0.1–1.0 minimal; 1.1–1.9 mild; 2.0–4.9 moderate; ≥ 5.0 marked. In this study most cases were in the "minimal" category; moderate and marked inflammation did not occur. Attention: in diffuse inflammation there are no foci, so the index comes out as 0 — this does not mean there is no inflammation.

t: Basso classification: types of myocarditis
n: Basso classification: types of myocarditis. The classification is based on the guidance of the Association for European Cardiovascular Pathology, AECVP, and is adapted from Basso's work. A focus is at least 10 inflammatory cells. Sparse foci without damage are considered borderline myocarditis. In focal myocarditis there is at least 1 focus and damage. In multifocal, there are several foci in one section or foci in many sections. In acute diffuse, widespread infiltration without foci is seen. Between the groups, only acute diffuse myocarditis gave a significant difference, P = 0.021.

t: Quick question 4: classification and index
n: The fourth quick question, classification and index. Question 1: what is the difference between focal and multifocal myocarditis? Focal is at least one focus with damage. Multifocal is several foci in one section or foci with damage in many sections. Question 2: how is the inflammation index calculated? We divide the total number of foci by the total number of sections, the Kitulwatte method. Interpretation: 0 none; 0.1–1.0 little; 1.1–1.9 mild; 2.0–4.9 moderate; ≥5.0 marked inflammation. Attention: risk of error — in diffuse inflammation there are no foci and the index comes out as 0. This does not mean there is no inflammation; on the contrary, it is the most severe form.

t: Myocyte damage and immunohistochemistry
n: Myocyte damage and immunohistochemistry. Myocyte damage is vacuolation, fragmentation or disintegration of the cardiomyocyte next to inflammation. A necrotic cardiomyocyte may be recognised as a thin, slightly eosinophilic cell remnant. The predominant cell type was determined with haematoxylin and eosin and with CD45, CD68 and myeloperoxidase stains. CD45 identifies lymphocytes, CD68 macrophages, and MPO neutrophil and eosinophil granulocytes.

t: Results: distribution and degree of severity
n: Results: distribution and degree of severity. Of the 79 cases, in 17, that is 21.5%, the cardiac inflammation was diffuse. The inflammation index was minimal, 0.1–1.0, in most; moderate and high degrees did not occur. Between the groups only diffuse acute myocarditis gave a difference: 9 and 7 in groups 2 and 3, 1 case in group 1, P = 0.021. In the table, the minimal index was 24/27 in group 1, 17/29 in group 2 and 16/23 in group 3.

t: Myocardial sampling and location of foci
n: Myocardial sampling and location of foci. Number of sampling sites: in group 1 an average of 5.6, in group 2 8.3, in group 3 7.8; the difference was significant only between groups 1 and 2. In almost all cases the right and left ventricles, the anterior, lateral and posterior walls, and the interventricular septum were sampled; the conduction system in 13 cases. In non-diffuse cases the mean number of foci was 2.6 in group 2 and 1.8 in group 3; P = 0.375, the difference not significant. Foci were most often in the wall of the left ventricle; of the 13 cases in which the conduction system was sampled, foci were found there too in 3; both atria in only 1 case.

t: Infiltrate type and other histological features
n: Infiltrate type and other histological features. In group 1 the infiltrate was lymphocytic in almost all, 26/27; one case showed a mixed type. In group 3 too the lymphocytic type predominated, 18/23. In group 2 the type was the most varied: lymphocytic in only 13/29. In this group mixed, neutrophilic, eosinophilic and giant cell inflammation also occurred. Myocyte damage, 78%, 76% and 70%, oedema, fibrosis and haemorrhage gave no reliable difference between groups.

t: Myocyte damage and genetic/toxicological testing
n: Myocyte damage and genetic and toxicological testing. Myocyte damage has historically been regarded as the feature that separates significant from insignificant inflammation, by the Dallas criteria and the AECVP. Casali and colleagues found myocyte damage to distinguish fatal myocarditis; in this study, however, it may be an incidental finding, 78%, 76%, 70%. Papadakis: in myocarditis with "mild" changes, focal or borderline, in sudden cardiac death there is hereditary disease in 51%, and in an entirely normal heart in 47%. Therefore stopping the investigation at a diagnosis of myocarditis is dangerous; a low threshold is set for genetic and toxicological testing.

t: Attention: index 0 ≠ no inflammation
n: Attention: index 0 does not mean there is no inflammation. In diffuse inflammation there are no separate foci, so the calculated index comes out as 0. This is misleading: a value of 0 gives the impression of no inflammation, whereas the diffuse form is the most severe type. The index, that is the number of foci divided by the number of sections, should be applied only to non-diffuse types. The value of low indices is limited; the index gives more information at high values.

t: Case analysis: incidental or fatal myocarditis
n: Case analysis: incidental or fatal myocarditis. Situation: heart sections show several foci of inflammation and myocyte necrosis. No other histological cause of death has been found. Attention: multiple foci and myocyte damage also occurred in clearly unnatural death, in group 1, that is they may be incidental. Question: can this myocarditis be called the cause of death? What would the next steps be? Guide: exclude other causes, that is toxicology, genetics, clinical history, circumstances of the case. The diffuse acute form is considerably more reliable.

t: Reliability of the study: intra-observer agreement
n: Reliability of the study: intra-observer agreement. All histological re-review was carried out by one researcher; the second review was done at least 4 weeks later. Agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa; κ > 0.80 was regarded as strong agreement. For the number of foci κ = 0.85, myocyte damage 0.96, oedema 1.00, fibrosis 0.88, haemorrhage 0.92. The groups were compared with chi-square, Fisher's exact test or the Kruskal–Wallis test; P < 0.05 was taken as significant.

t: Limitations and comprehensive investigation
n: Limitations and comprehensive investigation. Genetic testing and family history were not carried out, so predisposition to arrhythmia was not assessed. In clinical autopsies a toxicological cause was not excluded; comorbid diseases made interpretation difficult. Over-assessment may complicate legal proceedings and even unjustifiably exonerate a suspect. The chain of comprehensive investigation is as follows: examination and organ histology, clinical history and circumstances of the case, toxicology and biochemistry, genetics and virology, and finally a cautious conclusion.

t: Remember: comparing lung and heart features
n: Remember: we compare lung and heart features. DAD alone does not determine the cause of death; ante-mortem and forensic medical data are assessed together. In the lung, hyaline membrane and alveolar exudate, and the exudative and proliferative phases are examined; alveolar fibrin indicates the proliferative phase. In the heart, there are foci of at least 10 cells and myocyte damage; the types are borderline, focal, multifocal and diffuse. In myocarditis the diffuse acute form is important and was the only feature that distinguished incidental inflammation. Remember: one feature is not one conclusion; first exclude other causes.

t: Conclusion and practical recommendations
n: Conclusion and practical recommendations. Histology alone cannot reliably distinguish incidental inflammation of the myocardium from significant inflammation. Only diffuse inflammation showed a difference. In assessment, all autopsy results, additional tests, that is toxicology, virology and genetics, and the circumstances of death are considered together. Diffuse alveolar damage by itself does not state the cause of death. Its absence does not exclude acute respiratory distress syndrome. If a broad investigation is impossible, one should be cautious about drawing a firm conclusion on the cause and mechanism of death.
